18  documents that refer or relate to sales of Bac-Stop, whether or not it was sold by or 
19  for [the alleged partnership between Plaintiffs and Defendant], including, without 

20  limitation, invoices, bill of sales [sic], bill of ladings [sic], purchase orders and/or 
1  any other document evidence the sale [sic] of Bac Stop,” ECF No. 32-1 at 3-4 
2  (underlining in original), for sales made in “the period of March 15, 2020[,] 

3  through September 17, 2020,” ECF No. 32-3 at 1 (underlining in original), in 
4  “Washington, Oregon, California, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, and Montana,” ECF 
5  No. 32-4 at 1-2.  This request was based on Plaintiffs’ contention that they 

6  acquired new customers from these states who bought Defendant’s Bac Stop  
7  product in this timeframe, and that the records from these sales may have omitted 
8  reference to Plaintiffs due to administrative oversight.  ECF No. 30 at 3-4; see also 
9  ECF No. 43 at 2-4.  The timeframe and geographic limitations were key to  

10  defining the appropriate scope of RFP No. 3, as Plaintiffs were apparently unable 
11  to identify the relevant customers.  See ECF Nos. 32-4, 32-5.

13  burdensome, ECF No. 41, but at the October 15, 2024, discovery hearing, defense 
14  counsel could not explain what type and magnitude of burden Defendant would 
15  face in responding to RFP 3.  The Court directed Defendant to respond to RFP 3 
16  under the time-period and geographic limitations to which Plaintiffs had already 

17  agreed.  ECF No. 52 at 3.  Given the delay caused by the discovery dispute, the 
18  Court directed the parties to propose an amended scheduling order based on their 
19  determination of a feasible pretrial schedule.  Id. at 2.

8  $411,768.38.  ECF No. 79 at 14.  The Court concluded that Plaintiffs had not 
9  established that Mr. Harvey had personal knowledge about facts related to 

10  unattributed Bac Stop sales, was competent to testify on that subject, or had any 
11  basis besides speculation for his attestation of the amount of those damages.  ECF 
12  No. 96 at 15.  Plaintiffs offered nothing else except for their experts’ reports on 

13  unallocated Bac Stop damages, in which their experts explicitly stated that their 
14  opinions on unallocated Bac Stop damages depended entirely on Mr. Harvey’s

18  federal and Washington courts require competent evidence to support a claim for 
19  damages, as Plaintiffs acknowledge.  See ECF No. 109 at 11 (quoting Fed. Signal 

20  Corp. v. Safety Factors, Inc., 886 P.2d 172, 188 (Wash. 1994)).  If they relied on a

2       When a defendant moves for dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction

11  allegations of its complaint,’ but uncontroverted allegations in the complaint must 
12  be taken as true.”  Mavrix Photo, Inc. v. Brand Techs., Inc., 647 F.3d 1218, 1223 

13  (9th Cir. 2011) (quoting Schwarzenegger, 374 F.3d at 800).  If any conflict exists 
14  between the parties’ evidence, the court must resolve it in the plaintiff’s favor. 
15  AT&T v. Compagnie Bruxelles Lambert, 94 F.3d 586, 588 (9th Cir. 1996).    
16       A federal district court sitting in diversity may exercise personal jurisdiction 

17  “to the extent the forum state’s laws constitutionally provide.”  Metro. Life Ins. Co. 
18  v. Neaves, 912 F.2d 1062, 1065 (9th Cir. 1990).  Washington’s long-arm statute 
19  authorizes courts to exercise jurisdiction over nonresident defendants to the “full 

20  extent” of the Due Process Clause.  Easter v. Am. W. Fin., 381 F.3d 948, 960 (9th 
1  Cir. 2004) (citing Shute v. Carnival Cruise Lines, Inc., 783 P.2d 78, 79-80 (Wash. 
2  1989)); see also Corker v. Costco Wholesale Corp., 585 F. Supp. 3d 1284, 1290 

3  (W.D. Wash. 2022).  Accordingly, the Court need only determine whether

8  play and substantial justice.’”  Int’l Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U.S. 310, 316 
9  (1945) (quoting Milliken v. Meyer, 311 U.S. 457, 463 (1940)).

14    C. General Jurisdiction                                                 
15       “Two authorities govern a federal court’s exercise of personal jurisdiction 
16  over a defendant: the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause and the long 

17  arm statute of the state in which the district court sits.”  Briskin v. Shopify, Inc., 87 
18  F.4th 404, 411 (9th Cir. 2023).  The Ninth Circuit has interpreted Washington’s 
19  long-arm statute, RCW 4.28.185, to “permit[] the exercise of jurisdiction to the full 

20  extent of the due process clause.”  Easter v. Am. W. Fin., 381 F.3d 948, 960 (9th 
1  Cir. 2004) (citation omitted); see also Failla v. FixtureOne Corp., 336 P.3d 1112, 
2  1116 (Wash. 2014) (en banc) (noting that Washington’s long-arm statute is 

3  “designed to be coextensive with federal due process”).                   
4       “A court may exercise general jurisdiction ‘only when a defendant is 
5  essentially at home in the state.’”  Impossible Foods, Inc. v. Impossible X LLC, 80 

6  F.4th 1079, 1086 (9th Cir. 2023) (quoting Ford Motor Co. v. Mont. Eighth Jud. 
7  Dist. Ct., 141 S. Ct. 1017, 1024 (2021)).  The inquiry is whether a foreign 
8  “corporation’s affiliations with the State are so continuous and systematic as to 
9  render it essentially at home in the forum State.”  Daimler AG v. Bauman, 571 U.S. 

10  117, 138-39 (2014) (citation, quotation marks, and alteration omitted).  “The 
11  paradigm all-purpose forums for general jurisdiction are a corporation’s place of 
12  incorporation and principal place of business.”  Id. at 118 (citing Goodyear Dunlop 

13  Tires, 564 U.S. at 924).  However, “in an ‘exceptional case,’ a corporate 
14  defendant’s operations in another forum ‘may be so substantial and of such a 
15  nature as to render the corporation at home in that state.’”  BNSF Ry. Co. v. Tyrrell, 
16  581 U.S. 402, 413 (2017) (quoting Daimler, 571 U.S. at 139 n.19).  This is a high 

17  standard—for example, in BNSF Ry. Co., the Supreme Court held there was no 
18  general jurisdiction even though the defendant had more than 2,000 miles of 
19  railroad track and employed more than 2,000 employees in the forum state.  Id. at 

20  414.  The standard is so particular because it opens the defendant to suit on causes 
1  of action that are unrelated to their activities in the forum state.  King v. Am. 
2  Family Mut. Ins. Co., 632 F.3d 570, 579 (9th Cir. 2011).

7  Jersey.  ECF No. 1 at 4; ECF No. 2 at 2; ECF No. 15 at 4.                 
8       Nor have Plaintiffs established that this is an “exceptional case” for 
9  extending general jurisdiction beyond the paradigmatic bases.  Besides contending 

10  that Arxada, LLC purchased, supervises, and manages Enviro Tech (an allegation

16  Plaintiffs offer further arguments regarding Arxada, LLC’s contacts with  

17  Washington.4  But the evidence before the Court ultimately shows little, if any,

1  “Every contract imposes upon each party a duty of good faith and fair dealing in its 
2  performance and its enforcement.”  Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 205 (Am. 

3  Law. Inst. 1981).  This duty “arises when one party has discretionary authority to 
4  determine a future contract term.”  Rekhter v. State, Dep’t of Social and Health 
5  Servs., 323 P.3d 1036, 1041 (Wash. 2014).  The duty prevents contracting parties 

6  from engaging in conduct that frustrates the other party’s right to the benefits of 
7  the contract.  Woodworkers of Am. v. DAW Forest Prods. Co., 833 F.2d 789, 795 
8  (9th Cir. 1987).  Although the duty of good faith and fair dealing is present in 
9  every contract, the covenant “creates obligations only in relation to the agreed 

10  terms of the contract.”  Rekhter, 323 P.3d at 1041.  Examples of potential 
11  violations of the duty of good faith and fair dealing include: 1) evading the spirit of 
12  the bargain; 2) willfully rendering imperfect performance; 3) interference with or 

13  failing to cooperate in the other party’s performance; abusing discretion granted 
14  under the contract; or 5) performing the contract without diligence.  Microsoft 
15  Corp. v. Motorola, Inc., 963 F. Supp. 2d 1176, 1184 (W.D. Wash. 2013).    
16       Enviro Tech correctly argues that the implied covenant of good faith and fair 

17  dealing does not impose a general, “free-floating obligation of good faith” upon it.  
18  See id.  Rather, the obligation must arise out of a specific term of the Agreement 
19  that gave Enviro Tech discretion over a future term.  See id. at 1041-42.  Plaintiffs 

20  have not alleged in the Complaint that any term of the Agreement gave Enviro 
1  Tech the discretionary authority to determine a future contract term and does not 
2  specify which terms were allegedly performed in bad faith.  Plaintiffs allege only

4  Plaintiffs have failed to articulate how any of the four alleged acts they complain

7  795.

10  would be futile and the claim is dismissed with prejudice.

.  Examples of potential 
11  violations of the duty of good faith and fair dealing include: 1) evading the spirit of 
12  the bargain; 2) willfully rendering imperfect performance; 3) interference with or 

13  failing to cooperate in the other party’s performance; abusing discretion granted 
14  under the contract; or 5) performing the contract without diligence.  Microsoft 
15  Corp. v. Motorola, Inc.,

1       “A conversion is the act of willfully interfering with any chattel, without 
2  lawful justification, whereby any person entitled thereto is deprived of the

143 F.3d 502

631 P.2d 937
, 940

12  ownership nor a possessory interest in the funds . . . .”).  Moreover, “there can be 

13  no conversion of money unless it was wrongfully received by the party charged 
14  with conversion, or unless such party was under obligation to return the specific 
15  money to the party claiming it.”  Pub. Util. Dist. No. 1 of Lewis Cnty. v. Wash. 
16  Pub. Power Supply Sys.,
705 P.2d 1195, 1211

713 P.2d 17 1109
